explanations.explanation: Twelve it is, friend. God tells Moses, Israel's leader, to take “…twelve staffs, one from the leader of each tribe.” (Numbers 17:2) Twelve tribes, twelve leaders, twelve sticks. Nobody gets left out of this one.

Seven is a fair guess, friend, but the count here runs bigger. God asks for “…twelve staffs, one from the leader of each tribe.” (Numbers 17:2) Moses ends up with “…twelve staffs in all.” (Numbers 17:6) Stopping at seven is like counting a tray of cookies and walking off halfway down the rows.

Ten is a nice round number, friend, but this story goes with twelve. God asks for one staff from the leader of each tribe, and Moses ends up with “…twelve staffs in all.” (Numbers 17:6) Ten would leave two leaders out, and I bet they'd have a LOT to say about that.

That's right, baker. God says, “Write each man’s name on his staff…” (Numbers 17:2) So every leader's stick has his own name on it. It's like putting your name on your cookie box at the bake sale. When it's time to pick up, there's no arguing over whose is whose.

Careful, friend, because this one is True. God tells Moses, “Write each man’s name on his staff…” (Numbers 17:2) Each leader gets his own name on his own staff. It's like writing your name on your charger at work, so nobody walks off with it and acts surprised.

That's the one, baker. Levi is a tribe too, so it gets a staff, and God says “…write Aaron’s name on the staff of Levi…” (Numbers 17:3) The reason He gives is “…there must be one staff for the head of each tribe.” Nobody gets a blank staff in this lineup.

Korah is a name that might be stuck in your head right now, I bet. But God doesn't say his name here. The text says to write “…Aaron’s name on the staff of Levi…” (Numbers 17:3) Korah's name isn't part of those instructions.

Eleazar is a name you might know, friend, but this verse doesn't use it. God says, “…write Aaron’s name on the staff of Levi…” (Numbers 17:3) His reason is “…there must be one staff for the head of each tribe.” So Levi's staff gets Aaron's name, not Eleazar's. Eleazar doesn't get a staff. He just gets to watch twelve sticks sit there overnight, like a very quiet cookie sheet.

Sprout is right, baker! God says, “The staff belonging to the man I choose will sprout…” (Numbers 17:5) A staff sprouting. Sticks don't usually do that, friend. I've pressed a lot of dough in my day, and nothing I own has ever sprouted.

explanations.answer: It will turn into a snake
explanations.explanation: I see where that comes from. Aaron's staff did become a serpent once, when he threw it down before Pharaoh, Egypt's king (Exodus 7:10). But that's a different story. This time God says the chosen man's staff “will sprout.” (Numbers 17:5)

Flames would be dramatic, I'll give you that. But that's not what God says here. He says, “The staff belonging to the man I choose will sprout…” (Numbers 17:5) It's growing, not burning. Burning is my department, and mine only happens by accident.

That's right, friend. God says, “…I will rid Myself of the constant grumbling of the Israelites against you.” (Numbers 17:5) The word is constant. The grumbling has been going on and on, and God says what He plans to do about it.

This one is True. God really does say, “…I will rid Myself of the constant grumbling of the Israelites against you.” (Numbers 17:5) The grumbling was against Moses, and God says it's constant. So He gives them a sign they can see, with their own eyes.

Levi it is, baker! Moses enters the Tent of the Testimony and sees that “…Aaron’s staff, representing the house of Levi…” had changed. (Numbers 17:8) Out of all twelve staffs, the text points to that one. That's the staff with Aaron's name on it.

Judah's a big name, so I see why you'd pick it. But the text names a different staff: “…Aaron’s staff, representing the house of Levi…” (Numbers 17:8) That's the one Moses sees has sprouted. Levi's staff, not Judah's.

Reuben's a fair guess, friend, but that's not the staff the text points to. It says “…Aaron’s staff, representing the house of Levi…” had sprouted. (Numbers 17:8) Levi's staff is the one with Aaron's name on it (Numbers 17:3).

All of it, baker! Moses walks in the next day and sees that Aaron's staff “…had sprouted, put forth buds, blossomed, and produced almonds.” (Numbers 17:8) You know when you come back the next day and there's a pile of emails waiting? Moses came back to a dry stick that had buds, blossoms and almonds. NOW that's a morning surprise.

Grapes, figs and pomegranates make a nice fruit basket. But the text lists something else. It says the staff “…had sprouted, put forth buds, blossomed, and produced almonds.” (Numbers 17:8) So there was no fruit basket on that stick. It was all almonds.

Thorns would have been a rough surprise, friend. The text says nothing about thorns, thistles or olives. It says the staff “…had sprouted, put forth buds, blossomed, and produced almonds.” (Numbers 17:8) Buds, blossoms and almonds, all on one stick.

It's a natural thing to think. It's his staff, and it just sprouted, so you'd expect Aaron to get it back. But the LORD says, “Put Aaron’s staff back in front of the Testimony, to be kept as a sign for the rebellious…” (Numbers 17:10) The staff doesn't go home with Aaron. It stays right there.

That's right, baker. The LORD tells Moses, “Put Aaron’s staff back in front of the Testimony…” (Numbers 17:10) It doesn't go back to Aaron's hand. It goes back in front of the Testimony, “…to be kept as a sign for the rebellious…”

Rebellious is right, friend! The LORD says the staff is to be “…kept as a sign for the rebellious…” (Numbers 17:10) It's a sign meant for the ones who rebel. The staff stays put, and the sign stays up.

Priests is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't the word God uses here. He says the staff is to be “…kept as a sign for the rebellious…” (Numbers 17:10) He gives the purpose too: “…so that you may put an end to their grumbling against Me, lest they die.” So this sign isn't a trophy for the priests. It's a reminder set out for the grumblers. I've kept a lot of things in a drawer, but never a sign like that.

Foreigners didn't make it into this verse, friend. The LORD says the staff is “…to be kept as a sign for the rebellious…” (Numbers 17:10) The word is rebellious. This is about the Israelites who keep grumbling.

Right you are, baker. God tells Moses to keep the staff there “…so that you may put an end to their grumbling against Me, lest they die.” (Numbers 17:10) Earlier the grumbling was against Moses. Now God says it is against Him. That's what the LORD Himself says, and I'm not about to add anything to it.

This one is True. When God explains the sign, He says it's so that Moses “…may put an end to their grumbling against Me, lest they die.” (Numbers 17:10) Earlier He spoke of grumbling against Moses. Here He says it's against Him.

That's right, baker. The LORD says the sign is there to “…put an end to their grumbling against Me, lest they die.” (Numbers 17:10) The words are “…lest they die.” That's a serious line. I think it shows how much is at stake.
Scattered sounds like it could fit, but that's not what God says. The text says the grumbling is to end “…lest they die.” (Numbers 17:10) That's the reason He gives, and I won't add any others.
Enslaved isn't what God says here, friend. He says the grumbling is to end “…lest they die.” (Numbers 17:10) Life or death is the whole point of this verse.

explanations.answer: That they are all lost and perishing
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The Israelites declare, “Look, we are perishing! We are lost; we are all lost!” (Numbers 17:12) They say it three different ways, back to back. I think they're scared. That's my guess, not the text, but the words themselves sound scared.

explanations.answer: That they will gladly follow Aaron
explanations.explanation: That would be a tidy ending, but the people don't say it here. Their words are, “Look, we are perishing! We are lost; we are all lost!” (Numbers 17:12) Nothing in these verses mentions them following Aaron.

explanations.answer: That they want to go back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt doesn't come up in what they say here, friend. What they say is, “Look, we are perishing! We are lost; we are all lost!” (Numbers 17:12) They're crying out about what's in front of them, and the words are right there on the page.

It's the other way around, friend. The Israelites say, “Anyone who comes near the tabernacle of the LORD will die.” (Numbers 17:13) They are not saying anyone is safe there. I think that tells you how worried they are.

That's right, baker. The Israelites say, “Anyone who comes near the tabernacle of the LORD will die.” (Numbers 17:13) They say the opposite of safe. I think that tells us how scared they are after what they've just seen.
